summary: Sirach 13 warns a vulnerable reader about unequal relationships with the proud, mighty, and rich. It uses comparisons such as pitch, an earthen pot beside a kettle, and a wolf with a lamb to picture how power can exploit weakness. The chapter ends by observing how wealth and poverty affect public treatment, while still qualifying that riches are not evil if joined to no sin.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach applying wisdom to social inequality, patronage, and speech around powerful people. It belongs to the book’s larger effort to form practical judgment in ordinary relationships, especially where power is uneven.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson’s translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, and daily life shaped by unequal social and economic relationships.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction using poetic comparisons, warnings, and maxims; the World English Bible represents a shorter Greek-based form.

outline.heading: Contact with pride and power
outline.note: The chapter opens with warnings against close fellowship with the proud, mighty, and rich, using pitch and mismatched vessels as images of danger.

outline.heading: How the rich exploit the poor
outline.note: The speaker describes a rich person who wrongs, threatens, uses, deceives, shames, and abandons someone with less power.

outline.heading: Caution around a mighty host
outline.note: The reader is told to be reserved, avoid pressing too close or standing too far off, distrust flattering talk, and guard private matters while walking in danger.

outline.heading: Like with like
outline.note: A series of comparisons says creatures and people associate with their own kind, then applies that pattern to sinners and the godly, rich and poor, proud and lowly.

outline.heading: Public bias toward wealth
outline.note: The chapter contrasts how rich and humble or poor people are treated when they fall, speak, or stumble.

outline.heading: Wealth, poverty, and the heart
outline.note: The ending qualifies the chapter’s warnings: riches can be good without sin, poverty is called evil only by the ungodly, and the heart shows itself in the countenance.

keyVerses.text: He who touches pitch will be defiled. He who has fellowship with a proud man will become like him.
keyVerses.why: This opening line gives the chapter’s first image: close contact can change or contaminate a person’s conduct.

keyVerses.text: Don’t take up a burden above your strength. Have no fellowship with one who is mightier and richer than yourself. What fellowship would the earthen pot have with the kettle? The kettle will strike, and the pot will be dashed in pieces.
keyVerses.why: The verse states the main warning about unequal power and illustrates it with fragile pottery beside a hard vessel.

keyVerses.text: A rich man speaks, and all keep silence. They extol what he says to the clouds. A poor man speaks, and they say, “Who is this?” If he stumbles, they will help to overthrow him.
keyVerses.why: This verse sharply summarizes the chapter’s concern with unequal social response to rich and poor people.

keyVerses.text: Riches are good if they have no sin. Poverty is evil only in the opinion of the ungodly.
keyVerses.why: This sentence prevents a simple reading that wealth itself is condemned or poverty itself is morally bad.

themes: the heart shown in the countenance

questions.question: What is the chapter mainly warning about?
questions.answer: It warns about relationships where one person has much more status, wealth, or power than another. The concern is not ordinary friendship across difference, but fellowship that exposes the weaker person to exploitation, shame, or abandonment.

questions.question: What does “pitch” mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse, pitch is something that defiles the one who touches it. The comparison introduces the idea that close contact with a proud person can leave a mark on the other person’s character or situation.

questions.question: Why compare a person to an earthen pot beside a kettle?
questions.answer: The image pictures a fragile object beside a harder one. The verse says the kettle will strike and the pot will be dashed in pieces, so the point is the danger of entering an unequal relationship without enough strength to withstand the other party.

questions.question: Is the chapter saying rich people are always evil?
questions.answer: No. The chapter repeatedly criticizes exploitative rich people and social systems that favor them, but verse 24 adds a qualification: “Riches are good if they have no sin.” The chapter’s target is wealth joined to pride, harm, manipulation, or public injustice, not wealth as an automatic moral category.

questions.question: Why does the advice in verses 9-11 sound so cautious around a powerful person?
questions.answer: The text assumes the powerful host may test, flatter, or discard the weaker guest. The reader is told to be reserved, not to press too close, not to stand too far off, and not to believe many words. This is social survival advice inside an unequal setting, not a general command to fear every person with authority.

questions.question: What is difficult about the animal comparisons in verses 17-19?
questions.answer: The comparisons are stark: wolf and lamb, hyena and dog, lions and wild donkeys. Readers differ over how to apply such images, because they can sound as though social separation is natural and fixed. Within this chapter, the images mainly serve the warning that predatory power can endanger the vulnerable, especially the poor.

questions.question: Does the chapter treat poverty as a moral failure?
questions.answer: No. Verse 24 says poverty is evil only “in the opinion of the ungodly,” which distances the chapter from blaming the poor. The surrounding verses criticize how the poor and humble are dismissed, rebuked, or pushed away even when they speak wisely.

questions.question: Why is verse 14 blank in this edition?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verse 14 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

questions.question: How does the ending about the heart and countenance fit the chapter?
questions.answer: After many warnings about outward status, the chapter ends by turning to what a person’s face may show about the heart. It says the heart changes the countenance for good or evil, and that a cheerful countenance signals a prosperous heart. The final line about devising proverbs also reminds the reader that wise sayings require strenuous thinking, not quick slogans.

glossary.def: A substance used in the opening comparison; touching it is said to defile, illustrating how close fellowship can affect a person.
A fragile vessel in the comparison of unequal strength; it is dashed in pieces when struck by the kettle.
The stronger vessel in the comparison; it represents the more powerful party in an unequal relationship.
Fine food or treats in the scene where the powerful person shames the vulnerable guest until he has made him bare.
The face or outward expression; the chapter says it can change according to the heart.
